title: What does "scalable" actually mean for this system, and how would you prove it?
summary: Tests whether you can define scalability operationally — linear cost per added capacity, no hidden ceiling — instead of using it as a vague compliment for any design with more than one server.

slides.markdown:
"Is this scalable?" is a trap for candidates who use the word as an unexamined compliment — the moment you're asked to define it, a vague "yeah, it scales" collapses. Interviewers want an **operational definition**: adding capacity grows what the system can handle, roughly linearly, with no hidden ceiling.

By the end of this topic you'll be able to define scalability precisely, name where a specific design actually hits its ceiling, and back the claim with a number instead of an adjective.

slides.sectionTitle: Clarifying questions: scalable to what, along which dimension?
slides.markdown:
"Scalable" is meaningless without a target and an axis. Ask: **scalable to what number** — 10x today's load, or 1000x? — and **along which dimension** — more users, more data volume, or more requests per second, since a design can scale well on one axis and poorly on another.

A system that handles 100x more users gracefully might still choke at 10x more data per user if its indexes or storage layout were sized for the smaller case.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: define it operationally
slides.markdown:
The skeleton: define scalable as **"adding capacity increases what the system can handle, roughly linearly, with no hidden ceiling"** — not "it has a load balancer" or "it's on the cloud."

This definition gives you something falsifiable to check against any design: does doubling the nodes roughly double the throughput? If the answer is "no, because the database is still one instance," you've just found the honest answer to whether the system is actually scalable.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a design that scales linearly, then hits a hard ceiling
slides.markdown:
![Line chart of throughput vs nodes added, rising near-linearly for the app tier then flattening abruptly once the single database primary saturates](assets/scalability-ceiling-chart.svg)

The app tier genuinely scales — more nodes, proportionally more capacity — right up until the single database primary saturates, at which point adding more app nodes does nothing: they're all now waiting on the same maxed-out database.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: proving scalability with a number
slides.markdown:
Don't just claim it — **show the math**: "this handles 10k QPS on 10 nodes; adding 10 more nodes gets us to roughly 20k QPS, not diminishing returns, because the app tier is stateless and the database isn't yet saturated at that load."

That's a falsifiable, specific claim an interviewer can push on — "what happens at 40 nodes?" — versus "it's scalable," which invites no follow-up because it says nothing concrete to disagree with.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: testing the design against a stated target
slides.markdown:
Take the interviewer's actual target and run the arithmetic against it: if the target is 100k QPS and today's design does 10k QPS on 10 nodes, does going to 100 nodes really get you there — or does the database saturate at, say, 40 nodes' worth of load first?

This is where "scalable" stops being a label and becomes a real answer: you're not asserting the design scales, you're showing exactly how far it scales before something else has to change.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: near-linear scalability costs consistency or simplicity
slides.markdown:
| | Near-linear scalability | Simpler, less scalable design |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency | Often weaker — sharding, replicas, and caches trade off strict consistency | Easier — one source of truth |
| Operational complexity | Higher — routing, rebalancing, monitoring more moving parts | Lower — fewer failure modes to reason about |
| Ceiling | High, extends with added nodes | Hits a hard ceiling sooner |

**How to decide:** near-linear scalability is rarely free — it's usually bought with weaker consistency guarantees or more operational surface, so name that cost rather than presenting scalability as a pure win.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what's the actual next bottleneck, and at what number does it bite?
slides.markdown:
A design that scales for a while always has a next ceiling — name it specifically. "This scales to about 50k QPS on the current database; past that, single-primary write throughput becomes the limit, and the next lever is sharding by user ID."

Being able to name the *next* bottleneck, not just the current one, is what separates "I understand this design's limits" from "I've only thought about today's load."

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: is scaling reads the same problem as scaling writes?
slides.markdown:
No — and saying so shows real understanding rather than treating "scale" as one undifferentiated thing. **Reads** scale relatively easily via replicas and caching, since many copies of the same data can serve many readers. **Writes** are harder, since every write eventually has to land somewhere consistent, and adding more nodes doesn't automatically parallelize a single logical write stream the way it parallelizes reads.

A design can be highly scalable for reads and hit a wall on writes at a much lower number — always name which one you're claiming scalability for.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: using "scalable" as an unexamined adjective
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** calling a design "scalable" is itself a meaningful claim.

**Why it's wrong:** without naming the axis (users, data, requests) and the ceiling (where it stops being linear), "scalable" is a compliment, not an engineering statement — it invites no useful follow-up because it commits to nothing checkable.

**Correct model:** always pair the word with a number and an axis — "scales roughly linearly to N on this dimension, then hits Y as the next bottleneck." See [scalability fundamentals](scalability-fundamentals) for the underlying vocabulary.
